summary: This Best Current Practice describes iterative resolver behavior that sends large volumes of unnecessary queries to root and top-level domain servers. It offers implementation advice to resolver developers, drawn from observation of abnormal traffic at root servers and the com and net servers. It was later updated by RFC 9520.

plainLanguage.summary: The people who run the biggest domain name servers saw a large amount of pointless repeated traffic from programs that look up names. RFC 4697 lists eleven of those bad behaviors and tells the people who write such programs how to fix each one. It is advice for better software, not a change to the DNS protocol itself.

questions: why do resolvers send too many queries to root servers
what is a lame dns server
why do dns resolvers query the root servers too much
how long should a resolver avoid a lame server
subtitle: What the authors saw DNS resolvers doing wrong at the root and com/net servers, and how to stop it.

tldr.problem: Root and top-level domain name servers receive large volumes of repeated, useless queries, usually caused by a deficient resolver, stub resolver or application hitting an operational anomaly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs eleven observed misbehaviors, such as re-asking the parent for NS records, hammering lame servers, and retrying endlessly behind firewalls, and gives implementors a recommendation for each.
tldr.outcome: None of the advice changes the core DNS protocol, and the document is a Best Current Practice (BCP 123). It was later updated by RFC 9520.

facts.label: Load increase seen at com/net
facts.value: 50% when several dozen popular zones failed

today: RFC 4697 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 123) and has not been obsoleted, but it was updated by RFC 9520. Read the two together.

sections.title: Why Requeries Matter
sections.content:
RFC 4697 grew out of watching query traffic received by two of the thirteen root name servers and all thirteen com/net top-level domain (TLD) name servers. A large proportion of that traffic often consists of requeries: the same question (the same QNAME, QTYPE and QCLASS) asked repeatedly at an unexpectedly high rate, from a single IP address or from many addresses at once.

Analysis of requery events found that the cause is almost always a deficient iterative resolver, stub resolver or application implementation, combined with an operational anomaly. The implementation deficiencies include well-intentioned recovery attempts gone awry, insufficient caching of failures, giving up early when multiple levels of indirection must be followed, and aggressive retry. The anomalies include lame delegations, unusual glue records, and anything that makes every authoritative name server for a zone unreachable, such as denial of service attacks, crashes, maintenance, routing failures or congestion.

None of the recommended changes affects the core DNS protocol specification; the document is guidelines for implementors of iterative resolvers. The memo uses the term "iterative resolver" for the component of a recursive name server that sends queries, and "address record" to mean both A and AAAA records.

An iterative resolver is the part of a caching name server that sends queries out to other name servers. The name server part of the same software receives queries. The memo focuses on the sending part.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators of the root and com/net name servers kept seeing the same questions asked over and over for no good reason. They wrote down what the asking programs were doing wrong and how each mistake can be fixed.

sections.title: Re-asking the Parent for Delegation
sections.content:
The first misbehavior is an iterative resolver that, after discovering that none of a zone's name servers can answer, immediately sends a query for the zone's NS RRSet to one of the parent zone's name servers. Queries with QTYPE=NS are not required by the standard resolution algorithm in Section 4.3.2 of RFC 1034; this check is an implementation's own addition. When several dozen popular zones became unreachable on one occasion, the query load on the com/net name servers increased by 50%.

The memo argues the check is pointless. A resolver that has just followed a referral will get the same list of name servers back. And a resolver that once cached an NS RRSet from the zone's own servers holds more trustworthy data than the parent's delegation, as RFC 2181 explains, so the parent's answer would be less trustworthy than what is already cached. For the parent query to help, the zone's entire name server set would have to change and the parent would have to be updated, all within the TTL of the cached NS RRSet.

The recommendation is firm: an iterative resolver MUST NOT send a query for the NS RRSet of a non-responsive zone to that zone's parent's name servers. A non-responsive zone is one where every name server in the NS RRSet is lame (not authoritative), returns a server failure response (RCODE=2), or is dead or unreachable according to Section 7.2 of RFC 2308. Not every query to a parent is bad: if a cache holds an NS record but has lost the address record for an in-zone name server, the resolver must ask the parent for that glue address, but such a query does not have QTYPE=NS.
sections.plainLanguage: When every server for a zone is out of order, asking the parent zone again for the same list of servers does not help; the list has not changed. The RFC forbids this re-ask, with one exception: fetching a missing server address that only the parent has.

sections.title: Lame Servers and Failed Lookups
sections.content:
A lame server is a name server that has been delegated a zone but is not authoritative for it. Unlike a transient outage, this misconfiguration can last a long time, so repeatedly querying a known lame server is not useful. Iterative resolvers SHOULD cache lame servers. If they do, lame servers MUST be cached against the specific tuple of zone name, class and server IP address, and the implementation MUST refrain from querying the server for a configurable interval. A minimum interval of thirty minutes is RECOMMENDED.

The cache key matters: a name server can be lame for example.com yet properly authoritative for sub.example.com, so a server must not be automatically considered lame for subzones. There is also an exception for servers that appear lame only for certain query types, as described in RFC 4074: if all of a zone's name servers are marked lame, the iterative resolver SHOULD temporarily ignore their lameness status and query one or more of them.

Separately, some implementations cannot follow enough levels of indirection, such as a delegation whose name servers are themselves named under a zone that depends on further out-of-zone servers. Because the practice is widespread, iterative resolvers SHOULD be able to handle arbitrary levels of indirection from out-of-zone name servers, and SHOULD implement a level-of-effort counter to avoid loops. The best practice that avoids the issue entirely is to name at least one of a zone's name servers inside the zone itself.
sections.plainLanguage: A server that claims a zone but does not really serve it should be written down and skipped for a while, keyed by zone and address. But if every server for the zone looks bad, try again anyway, because some servers are only broken for one kind of question.

sections.title: Glue Fetching and Firewalls
sections.content:
A name server with glue fetching tries to include an address record for every NS record in the authority section of a referral, issuing its own queries when the addresses are missing. This causes problems for authoritative-only name servers whose administrators place them behind a network device that blocks incoming replies, expecting the server to receive only queries. All glue-fetching queries then go unanswered, and the observed implementations retried excessively: one com/net name server received hundreds of queries per second from a single such source.

The same pattern appears with iterative resolvers behind misconfigured firewalls that let queries out but drop the replies. The retransmissions are useless because the responses never arrive, they are sometimes sent at excessive rates, and they can continue for days or even weeks. Worse, the replies to these legitimate queries can trigger alarms on the sender's intrusion detection system, and administrators then complain that the root and TLD name servers are attacking them. The failure can stay hidden when stub resolvers also query another, working recursive name server; the memo notes that one popular stub resolver has a very aggressive retransmission schedule, including simultaneous queries to multiple servers.

The recommendations are that administrators SHOULD NOT place iterative resolvers behind a firewall that allows queries but blocks the resulting replies, that implementations avoid sending queries at excessive rates, and that implementations SHOULD support throttling logic to detect when queries are sent but no responses are received.
sections.plainLanguage: A server that shouts questions but wears earpluffs will keep shouting forever. Programs should notice when no answer ever comes back and calm down, and administrators should not block the answers on purpose.

sections.title: Zone Configuration Mistakes
sections.content:
Two mistakes in zone configuration put extra load on parent servers. The first is a missing trailing dot in the RDATA of a zone's NS records. A zone file for example.com that lists ns1.example.com without the final dot is parsed as ns1.example.com.example.com. Because NS records in the authority section of an authoritative answer are more trustworthy than the parent's referral (RFC 2181), the resolver replaces the good delegation with the bad one and then tries to resolve the nonexistent names, sending address queries to the com/net servers. An authoritative name server SHOULD issue a warning when one of a zone's NS records references a name server below the zone's apex and no matching address record exists in the zone and no delegated subzone could hold one.

The second mistake is a zero TTL on a zone's NS records. A zero TTL prohibits caching, so an iterative resolver must query the zone's parent's name servers every time it resolves a name in the zone. A zero TTL on an RRSet expected to change frequently is extreme but permissible, yet the memo says it rarely makes sense for a zone's NS RRSet, because changes to it must be coordinated with the parent and are typically rare. A low TTL is reasonable only in anticipation of an upcoming change. Authoritative name servers SHOULD issue a warning when loading a zone with a zero TTL on its NS RRSet.
sections.plainLanguage: Forgetting the final dot in a server address makes the name resolve to something that does not exist, so resolvers keep chasing it. Telling everyone to forget your server list immediately forces them to ask the parent every time. Servers should warn about both mistakes when they load the zone.

sections.title: Updates, Odd Queries and Server Choice
sections.content:
Section 2.8 covers unnecessary dynamic update messages. A popular dynamic update agent finds the closest enclosing zone by sending UPDATE messages to progressively higher-level zones, reaching the com/net servers and the root servers, and each failure teaches it nothing. Dynamic update agents SHOULD instead walk up the name space with SOA or NS queries, whose results can be cached, and send an UPDATE only after the appropriate zone is found. They SHOULD NOT probe with UPDATE messages.

The root name servers also receive many A record queries for names that look like IPv4 addresses, such as 192.0.2.1, answered with Name Error (RCODE=3). Each such name needs its own negative cache entry, so caching does not help much. The memo suggests delegating these numeric TLDs from the root zone to a separate set of servers, for instance the black hole servers of the AS 112 Project, following the usual root zone change procedures.

Root servers also receive recursive queries, with the Recursion Desired bit set, because users point stub resolvers at them even though they do not offer recursion. A stub resolver could send a test query and check for the RA bit to verify recursion support, and error reporting SHOULD be throttled so the user is not spammed. Finally, on name server selection, resolvers SHOULD treat all NS records in an RRSet equally rather than trusting their order, since the first-listed a.gtld-servers.net receives disproportionately more traffic than the other twelve com servers; use the whole RRSet, favor the best-performing server by response time, and periodically recheck all of a zone's servers instead of locking onto one.
sections.plainLanguage: Find the right zone with a plain question you can remember, not by sending updates to everyone in turn. Ask a simple test before trusting a server to do recursion, and take turns among a zone's servers instead of always using the first name on the list.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The iterative resolver misbehavior discussed in the document exposes the root and TLD name servers to increased risk of both intentional and unintentional denial of service attacks. The authors believe that implementing the recommendations will reduce the amount of unnecessary traffic seen at root and TLD name servers, and so reduce the opportunity for an attacker to use such queries to their advantage.

The RFC adds no new protocol features, and it states that there are no new internationalization considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Pointless repeated queries make the busiest name servers easier to overwhelm, on purpose or by accident. Cutting the waste lowers that risk. The RFC changes no protocol and raises no new language issues.

viz.caption: KEY RULES FOR LAME SERVER HANDLING (RFC 4697)

items.title: Cache the lame server
items.text: Key it by zone name, class and server IP address.

items.title: Wait before retrying
items.text: A minimum interval of thirty minutes is RECOMMENDED.

items.title: All lame is a special case
items.text: If every server for the zone is marked lame, query one or more anyway.

items.title: Do not spread to subzones
items.text: Lame for example.com does not mean lame for sub.example.com.
